newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa shares still seen good despite U.S. drop.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa shares still seen good despite U.S. drop.

text.p: The outlook for South African shares, knocked by Wall Street's recent huge fall, is still positive and the market could soon be approaching a buying opportunity, portfolio managers said on Monday.
A wave of selling hit the market in the first few minutes of trade as dealers offloaded stock in the wake of a 247.37 point drop to 7,694.66 points on the Dow Jones Industrial Average on Friday.
The New York fall, which many economists have long been predicting, was sparked by an earnings warnings from consumer products giant Gillette Co and another drop in the dollar.
But local portfolio managers said most of the early trade on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange was done by individual investors, while institutions were still holding back from panic buttons.

"There is no need for any panic whatsoever. If you look at the volumes that have been traded so far there has been no sell-off. It is more jobbers and individuals that have panicked," said Ryk de Klerk, senior portfolio manager and director at PSG Asset Management.
Portfolio managers said the U.S. market had been viewed as overbought and in dire need of a correction that would inevitably impact on local stocks.
But they said that South Africa's interest rate outlook was almost unique among major financial centres because it is heading for a cut rather than a rise.
They said Reserve Bank governor Chris Stals was facing increasing pressure to shave rates as the country's economy shows signs of slowing down.
"The pressure is just building. The real economy is getting weaker and weaker every day," de Klerk said.
Estimates for the timing of the cut ranged from the end of this month to as late as October and speculation on the move has been buoying the market for months.
Portfolio managers said the speculation would soon creep back and start moving stocks up again as selective blue-chips were starting to look cheap.
They said South African shares should bounce from their lows sooner than other world markets as they had been less overbought before Friday's fall.
Notable among stocks now starting to look cheap was diamond giant De Beers, which was already suffering a market hangover from poor interim results, and banking stocks like BOE and Investec.
"Our market was not nearly as expensive as the United States and so we will have less downside than them," said Denzil Newman, portfolio manager at Syfrets Managed Assets.
Newman said the local bourse would still be a bullish one even when the correction has been completed. "It is a bull market that is having a bit of a pullback. The question is by how much?" he said.

Some portfolio managers said the market would probably have to come off a little more to complete its correction, perhaps even losing ten percent from its recent peak levels. That would take the all-share index down to 6,854 and the industrials index to 8,384.
At 0915 GMT the all-share index was down 105.0 points to 7,334.8 and the industrials index was off 129.5 points to 8,991.4.
"There has been too much of what (U.S. Federal Reserve chairman) Alan Greenspan called "irrational exuberance". Friday's scare will have knocked a lot of that exuberance out," Newman said.
